title: Container With Most Water — two-pointer from ends, move shorter side.
shortTitle: Container With Most Water — Two-Pointer From Ends

s1_definition.profdef: The Container With Most Water problem treats an array of heights as vertical lines and asks for the maximum water a container formed by any two lines can hold. The area between two lines is the shorter of the two heights multiplied by the horizontal distance between them. The optimal solution uses two pointers starting at the ends, computes the area, records the best, and always moves the pointer at the shorter line inward, because moving the taller line could never increase the area. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India plots Rajesh's monthly balances as a bar chart, and an analyst wants to know which two months, used as the left and right walls of a tank, would hold the most water between them, as a visual measure of a sustained balance range. Two fingers start at the first and last month. The water held is limited by the shorter wall times the number of months apart. The analyst always moves the finger on the shorter wall inward, because keeping a short wall can never let the tank hold more, and records the largest tank seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start pointers at both ends, area is shorter height times width, and always move the shorter side inward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Container With Most Water problem treats an array of heights as vertical lines and asks for the maximum water a container formed by any two lines can hold. The area between two lines is the shorter of the two heights multiplied by the horizontal distance between them. The optimal solution uses two pointers starting at the ends, computes the area, records the best, and always moves the pointer at the shorter line inward, because moving the taller line could never increase the area. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India plots Rajesh's monthly balances as a bar chart, and an analyst wants to know which two months, used as the left and right walls of a tank, would hold the most water between them, as a visual measure of a sustained balance range. Two fingers start at the first and last month. The water held is limited by the shorter wall times the number of months apart. The analyst always moves the finger on the shorter wall inward, because keeping a short wall can never let the tank hold more, and records the largest tank seen.

**One line to remember:** Start pointers at both ends, area is shorter height times width, and always move the shorter side inward.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute force compares every pair of lines, computing each area, which is quadratic. The two-pointer method gets the same answer in a single linear pass by being clever about which pairs it can safely skip.

You put a left pointer at the first line and a right pointer at the last line. The area they form is the minimum of the two heights, because water spills over the shorter wall, multiplied by the width, which is the distance between the pointers. You record this area as the best so far. Then you move one pointer inward, and the rule is to move the pointer at the shorter line.

The reason you move the shorter line is the key insight. The area is capped by the shorter line. If you moved the taller line inward instead, the width would shrink and the height would still be capped by the same shorter line or something even shorter, so the area could never grow. By moving the shorter line you give up some width but you get the only chance of finding a taller limiting wall that could more than compensate. So moving the shorter line never discards a better answer, which is what makes the linear scan correct.

A senior point is proving you are not missing the optimum. The argument is that when you move the shorter pointer, every pair that used that shorter line with any line still between the pointers would have had an area no larger than the one you just computed, because the width was largest at this moment and the height was capped by that shorter line. So discarding those pairs is safe. This correctness argument is what interviewers want to hear, not just the mechanics.

Another senior point is the tie case. If the two lines are equal in height, moving either one is fine; moving both is also safe because any pair between them is capped by that same height with a smaller width. I usually move one side by convention and note the tie does not affect correctness.

For finance I use BigDecimal for the heights if they represent amounts, computing the limiting height with compareTo and the area with multiply, so the measure is exact. Widths are integer month distances. I also handle arrays of fewer than two lines by returning zero area since no container can be formed.

A small finance-domain example: `int l = 0, r = n - 1; BigDecimal best = ZERO; while (l < r) { BigDecimal h = min(height[l], height[r]); BigDecimal area = h.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(r - l)); if (area > best) best = area; if (height[l] < height[r]) l++; else r--; }` finds the maximum container area.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India visualises Rajesh's monthly closing balances as a bar chart, and an analytics feature highlights the two months that, used as the walls of a container, would hold the most water between them, as an intuitive measure of the widest sustained balance band. The feature must compute this quickly even for long histories. Finding the maximum container area with the two-pointer method is exactly this.

This is exactly how Container With Most Water works in Java — two pointers start at the ends and the shorter wall moves inward each step.

Problem 2 — Balances are exact BigDecimal amounts, so the limiting height and the area must be computed precisely, and the feature must return zero when there are fewer than two months since no container exists. This shows the money data-type care and the degenerate-case guard.

What the code will do: a `ContainerAnalyzer` with `maxContainerArea(BigDecimal[] heights)` using the two-pointer-from-ends technique, moving the shorter side and tracking the best area in BigDecimal. The demo computes the widest balance band for Rajesh's monthly balances.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the monthly balance heights are `1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7`.

Step 1: left starts at index zero with height `1`, right at index eight with height `7`. The limiting height is the smaller, `1`, and the width is eight, so the area is `1 * 8 = 8`, which becomes the best. Because the left height `1` is less than the right height `7`, we move left inward to index one.

Step 2: left at index one with height `8`, right at index eight with height `7`. Limiting height is `7`, width is seven, area is `49`, which beats the best, so best becomes `49`. Because the left height `8` is not less than the right height `7`, we move right inward to index seven.

Step 3: left at index one with height `8`, right at index seven with height `3`. Limiting height is `3`, width is six, area is `18`, which does not beat `49`. The right height `3` is smaller, so we move right inward to index six.

Step 4: left at index one with height `8`, right at index six with height `8`. Limiting height is `8`, width is five, area is `40`, which does not beat `49`. The heights are equal, so by convention we move right inward to index five.

Step 5: The scan continues, each step moving the shorter wall inward, computing areas like `5 * 4`, `5 * 3`, and so on, none of which beat `49`. Because we always move the shorter wall, we never discard a pair that could have given a larger area.

Step 6: The pointers eventually meet and the loop ends with best `49`. That is the maximum container area, the widest sustained balance band, found in a single linear pass with only two pointers and no nested comparison of all pairs.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T18:10:00Z INFO Max container area = 49
2026-10-26T18:10:00Z INFO Widest balance band area for Rajesh = 49
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input heights: [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]  left=0 right=8
    │
    ▼
  area = min(h[l],h[r]) × (r-l); move shorter side inward
    │ l0=1,r8=7 → min1×8=8   best=8   (move l, 1<7)
    │ l1=8,r8=7 → min7×7=49  best=49  (move r, 8>=7)
    │ l1=8,r7=3 → min3×6=18           (move r)
    │ l1=8,r6=8 → min8×5=40           (move r, tie)
    │ ... none beats 49, pointers converge
    ▼
  best = 49 (walls at index 1 and 8)
    ▼
  Output: widest sustained balance band area
```

```
      maxContainerArea contract:
        Pre:  heights may be null/<2 (returns 0)
        Post: max over pairs of min(h[l],h[r])×(r-l)
        Always move the SHORTER wall (keeps optimum reachable)

  ── State Diagram: Pointer Move ───────────────────────────

  [l<r] ──area=min×width; best=max──→ [h[l]<h[r]? l++ : r--]

  1. ContainerDemo.main()

  4.     → shorter side moves until l>=r

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Container With Most Water treats an array of heights as vertical walls and asks for the maximum water two walls can hold, where the area is the shorter of the two heights times the horizontal distance between them. I solve it with two pointers starting at the ends: I compute the area, record the best, and then move the pointer at the shorter wall inward. It is a single linear pass with constant space, beating the quadratic brute force that checks every pair.

The insight, and the part interviewers really want, is why I move the shorter wall. The area is capped by the shorter wall, so moving the taller wall inward would only shrink the width while the height stays capped by that same shorter wall or something shorter, which can never increase the area. Moving the shorter wall gives up some width but is the only way to possibly find a taller limiting wall that more than compensates, so it never discards a better answer. That correctness argument is what makes the linear scan valid, not just lucky.

I also handle the tie where both walls are equal by moving either side, since any pair between them is capped by the same height with smaller width, and I return zero for fewer than two walls since no container exists. For finance I use BigDecimal for the heights and the area so the measure is exact, taking the limiting height with min and compareTo.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to power a balance-band visualisation, highlighting the two months that, as the walls of a container, would hold the most water between them, giving Rajesh an intuitive picture of his widest sustained balance band, computed quickly even over long histories. Explaining the move-the-shorter-wall rule and the proof that it never misses the optimum shows the interviewer that I understand the greedy two-pointer deeply, which is exactly the depth this problem is designed to test.
